title: Sorting algorithms
subtitle: Eight ways to put numbers in order — and why “how many comparisons” is the question. The chapter derives the n log n lower bound, then builds every algorithm and counts its work on the same seven numbers.

why.title: Why sort, and what to ask of a sort
why.body:
Sorting is the most studied problem in computing because order makes everything else cheap: binary search needs sorted data, duplicates become adjacent, merging two sorted lists is linear, and a person can scan a sorted list at a glance. Formally, given records with keys k₁ … kₙ, produce a permutation in which the keys are non-decreasing.

Algorithms differ in properties beyond speed. A sort is internal if all data fits in memory and external if it must stream from disk (merge-based). It is in place if it needs only O(1) extra memory beyond the array. It is stable if records with equal keys keep their original relative order — vital when you sort by several keys in turn: sort a class list by name, then stably by grade, and students within each grade stay alphabetical; with an unstable sort the alphabetical order is scrambled. It is adaptive if it runs faster on nearly sorted input. And it is a comparison sort if it learns the order only by asking “is a < b?” — all of the algorithms except radix and counting sort.

We compare algorithms by counting comparisons and moves, using the same seven numbers throughout: 5 1 4 2 8 9 3. The C++ programs are real implementations that count their comparisons, and the cards show the same counts, so you can check each by hand.

bound.title: How fast can comparison sorting be? The n log n barrier
bound.body:
Before building algorithms it helps to know the target. Is O(n log n) merely the best we have found, or a hard limit? For algorithms that only compare keys it is a hard limit, and the proof is a lovely counting argument. Picture a sorting algorithm as a decision tree: each internal node is a comparison “is aᵢ < aⱼ?”, with two outgoing branches for yes and no; each leaf is the final answer — a particular ordering of the input. For the algorithm to be correct, every one of the n! possible orderings of n distinct keys must appear at some leaf. A binary tree of height h has at most 2ʰ leaves, so 2ʰ ≥ n!, and the worst-case number of comparisons — the height — is at least log₂(n!).

How big is log₂(n!)? Using Stirling’s approximation, n! ≈ (n/e)ⁿ, so log₂ n! ≈ n log₂ n − 1.44 n = Θ(n log n). A cruder bound is enough: n! has at least n/2 factors each ≥ n/2, so n! ≥ (n/2)^{n/2} and log₂ n! ≥ (n/2) log₂(n/2). The table shows the exact minimum for small n: sorting 5 items needs at least 7 comparisons, sorting 10 at least 22. Merge sort and heap sort meet this bound up to constants — they are asymptotically optimal. To beat n log n you must stop comparing and exploit the structure of the keys, as counting sort and radix sort do (section 7.10).
bound.steps: A comparison sort is a binary decision tree. Each of the n! input orderings must reach a different leaf, otherwise two different inputs would be given the same output permutation and one would be wrong. A binary tree of height h has at most 2^h leaves. Take logarithms: the worst-case number of comparisons h is at least log₂ n!. Bound the factorial from below by its largest n/2 factors.

bubble.title: Bubble sort
bubble.body:
Walk along the array comparing neighbouring pairs and swap any pair that is out of order. After one pass the largest element has “bubbled” to the end, like a bubble rising in water. Repeat for the unsorted part: n − 1 passes, the i-th scanning n − i pairs, so n(n − 1)/2 comparisons in total — O(n²). Adding an early exit (stop if a whole pass made no swap) makes the best case — an already sorted array — a single pass of n − 1 comparisons, so O(n). It is stable (equal elements are never swapped) and in place. The number of swaps equals the number of inversions (out-of-order pairs) in the input, which is why a reversed array is the worst case with n(n − 1)/2 swaps.

For 5 1 4 2 8 9 3 it makes 20 comparisons and 8 swaps (the program’s output agrees). Bubble sort is almost never used in practice; it is taught because it is easy to analyse and a good first example of an invariant: after pass i the last i elements are in their final positions.
bubble.steps: One pass of bubble sort on 5 1 4 2: compare (5,1) swap → 1 5 4 2; compare (5,4) swap → 1 4 5 2; compare (5,2) swap → 1 4 2 5. The largest value, 5, is now in its final place. Three comparisons and three swaps were used. Worst case n = 7 (reversed input): every comparison swaps; total comparisons n(n − 1)/2 = 21, swaps 21.

select.title: Selection sort
select.body: Divide the array into a sorted prefix (initially empty) and an unsorted rest. Repeatedly select the smallest element of the unsorted part and swap it into the first unsorted position. After i rounds the first i elements are the i smallest, in order. It always makes n(n − 1)/2 comparisons whatever the input (21 here) — it is not adaptive — but it makes at most n − 1 swaps (6 here), which matters when writing is expensive (flash memory, or moving big records). It is in place; the long-distance swap makes it unstable (swapping the 5 of 5 5′ 2 with the 2 places 5′ before 5).

insert.title: Insertion sort
insert.body: Pick up playing cards one at a time and slide each into the right place among those already in your hand. Insertion sort does just that: the prefix a[0..i−1] is sorted; take the next element as key, shift every larger element of the prefix one place right, and drop the key into the gap. For random data it makes about n²/4 comparisons and shifts — still O(n²) — but its virtues are real: it is stable, in place, adaptive (an already-sorted array costs only n − 1 comparisons, O(n)), and its inner loop is tiny. For these reasons it is the algorithm real libraries use for small arrays (typically fewer than 10–20 elements) inside faster recursive sorts. The count of shifts equals the number of inversions: for 5 1 4 2 8 9 3 that is 8 shifts and 13 comparisons.
insert.steps: Insert 2 into the sorted prefix 1 4 5 (array: 1 4 5 | 2 8 …). Compare 2 with 5 → shift; with 4 → shift; with 1 → stop. Two shifts and three comparisons for this key. The total shifts over the whole sort equal the number of inversions: 5-1, 5-4, 5-2, 5-3, 4-2, 4-3, 8-3, 9-3 = 8.

shell.title: Shell sort
shell.body: Insertion sort is slow because an element that is far from its place moves one position at a time. Donald Shell (1959) noticed that if we first sort elements that are far apart, large elements jump close to their destinations quickly. Shell sort performs insertion sort on the elements spaced h apart, for a decreasing sequence of gaps h (for example n/2, n/4, …, 1). Each pass leaves the array “h-sorted”; the final pass with h = 1 is plain insertion sort, but by then the array is nearly sorted, so it is fast. The running time depends entirely on the gap sequence: the halving sequence gives O(n²) in the worst case, Knuth’s sequence (1, 4, 13, 40, …) O(n^{3/2}), and cleverer sequences about O(n^{4/3}) — far better than quadratic and with no extra memory or recursion. It is not stable. For our seven numbers it needs 14 comparisons.

merge.title: Merge sort
merge.body: Two sorted lists can be merged into one in linear time by repeatedly taking the smaller of the two front elements. Merge sort turns this into a sorting algorithm: split the array in half, sort each half recursively, and merge the two sorted halves. The base case is an array of one element, already sorted. The recurrence is T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n: the recursion tree has log₂ n levels and each level does n work in merging, so T(n) = Θ(n log n) in every case — best, average and worst — which makes it dependable. It is stable (take from the left half on ties) but needs O(n) extra space for the merge buffer. It is the natural choice for linked lists (merging needs no extra space) and for external sorting, where data too large for memory is sorted in chunks and merged from disk. Our run takes 12 comparisons.
merge.steps: Why O(n log n)? Halving gives log₂ n levels and each level does O(n) merging work. For n = 1024 that is about 10 levels × 1024 ≈ 10 240 operations, versus 1 048 576 for n². Merging [1 4 5] and [2 8 9]: compare 1/2 → 1; 4/2 → 2; 4/8 → 4; 5/8 → 5; then copy 8, 9. Five comparisons for six elements, never more than n − 1.

quick.title: Quick sort
quick.body:
Tony Hoare’s quick sort (1960) does its work before the recursive calls rather than after. Choose a pivot element; partition the array so everything smaller than the pivot is to its left and everything larger to its right — the pivot is then in its final place — and recursively sort the two sides. There is no merge step and no extra array: partitioning is done in place by one scan. In the common Lomuto scheme the last element is the pivot, an index i marks the end of the “smaller” region, and each element smaller than the pivot is swapped into that region.

Performance depends on how balanced the partitions are. If each splits the array roughly in half, the recurrence is T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n — O(n log n), and in practice quick sort is the fastest general-purpose sort because its inner loop is tight and cache-friendly. If the pivot is always the smallest or largest element, one side has n − 1 elements and T(n) = T(n − 1) + n = O(n²): this happens on already-sorted input when the first or last element is the pivot. The run below sorts 1..8 and makes 28 = 8·7/2 comparisons, exactly the quadratic worst case. Remedies: choose the pivot at random, or as the median of three (first, middle, last), which makes the bad case astronomically unlikely and gives O(n log n) expected time. Quick sort is in place but needs O(log n) stack on average (O(n) worst case) and is not stable. For our seven numbers it takes 13 comparisons.
quick.steps: Best case: the pivot always lands in the middle, so each call splits n into two halves and partitioning costs n. Worst case: the pivot is the extreme element, so one subproblem is empty and the other has n − 1 elements. Even a lopsided but constant split, say 1:9, keeps the tree depth logarithmic (log_{10/9} n levels) with n work per level, so the cost stays O(n log n) — which is why random pivots work so well.

heapsort.title: Heap sort
heapsort.body: Last chapter’s heap makes a sort almost for free. Phase 1: arrange the array into a max-heap (parent ≥ children) with the O(n) bottom-up build. Phase 2: the largest element is at the root; swap it with the last element of the heap, shrink the heap by one — the largest is now in its final position — and sift the new root down to restore the heap property. Repeat n − 1 times. Each sift-down is O(log n), so heap sort is O(n log n) in the worst case, uses O(1) extra space, and has no bad inputs. It is not stable, and its scattered memory accesses make it slower than quick sort in practice; it is the choice when you need a guaranteed bound and no extra memory — in embedded systems, or as the fallback in introsort (quick sort that switches to heap sort if the recursion gets too deep). Our run needs 19 comparisons and 14 moves.

linear.title: Sorting without comparing: counting and radix sort
linear.body:
The n log n barrier holds only for comparison sorts. If the keys are small integers we can sort in linear time by using them as array indices. Counting sort for keys in 0…k: make a count array of size k + 1, count how many times each key occurs, then write the keys back in order (or, for records, turn the counts into starting positions by a prefix sum and place each record, which makes the sort stable). Time O(n + k), space O(k). It is superb when k is not much larger than n — sorting ages, exam marks, or the digits inside radix sort — and hopeless when k is huge (32-bit integers would need a 4-billion-entry array). The program sorts ten numbers in 0…8 by counting.

Radix sort extends the idea to larger keys by processing one digit at a time: distribute the numbers into ten buckets by the least significant digit, collect them in bucket order, then repeat on the next digit, up to the most significant. Each pass is a counting sort, and it must be stable so the order from earlier digits survives within each later bucket. With d digits and base k the cost is O(d·(n + k)). The card sorts 170 45 75 90 802 24 2 66 into 2 24 45 66 75 90 170 802 in three passes (units, tens, hundreds). Bucket sort spreads keys uniformly distributed over an interval into n buckets, sorts each with insertion sort, and concatenates: O(n) expected.

choose.title: Choosing a sort
choose.body: No algorithm wins every contest, so the choice follows from the constraints. Small arrays (under ~20 elements): insertion sort. General purpose, in memory: quick sort (with a good pivot) or the library’s introsort/Timsort. Need a worst-case guarantee and little memory: heap sort. Need stability or sorting linked lists or external files: merge sort (Python’s and Java’s object sorts are Timsort, a merge/insertion hybrid that exploits existing runs). Data nearly sorted: insertion sort or Timsort. Small integer keys: counting or radix sort. Writes are expensive: selection sort minimises swaps. The table collects the facts; everything in it follows from the analysis above.

summary.title: Summary
summary.body:
• Properties: stable, in place, adaptive, internal/external; comparison sorts need ≥ log₂ n! = Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case.
  • O(n²): bubble (adjacent swaps; n with early exit), selection (min each round; n − 1 swaps), insertion (shift into prefix; best for small or nearly sorted).
  • Shell sort: insertion sort with shrinking gaps, about O(n^{4/3})–O(n²) depending on gaps.
  • Merge sort: always n log n, stable, O(n) space; quick sort: n log n average, n² worst (sorted input with a fixed pivot), in place; heap sort: n log n worst case, in place, unstable.
  • Counting and radix sort beat n log n by not comparing: O(n + k) and O(d(n + k)), stable, for small integer keys.
